intro: From the UN failing to agree on autonomous weapons rules to Signal scrambling to block AI surveillance and a South Korean minister resigning over an AI cheating scandal, today's big theme is institutions racing — and often failing — to keep up with AI's reach into every corner of life. But it's not all friction: everyday tinkerers are using AI coding tools to hack their own gadgets, and a new wave of AI agents living in your text messages wants to handle your errands. Buckle in — today's digest covers the full spectrum, from geopolitical standoffs to the AI assistant that books your dinner reservations over SMS.

stories.title: Australia's fragile bipartisan AI regulation agreement faces end-of-year parliamentary test
stories.summary: Australia's parliament enters its final 2026 sitting week with a joint select committee report on AI expected Monday, signaling Labor's direction on AI regulation including datacentres and copyright. Whether fragile bipartisan agreement survives the legislative rush remains uncertain.
stories.opinion: Useful signal on how a mid-sized democracy is approaching AI governance, though the outcome is still unknown.

stories.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots to counter AI surveillance threat
stories.summary: Signal is restricting screenshot capabilities on Android and iOS in response to what president Meredith Whittaker calls the 'existential threat' of OS-level agentic AI surveillance. AI agents built into Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS can scan screen content, undermining Signal's privacy guarantees. Users can disable the setting, and Whittaker concedes the solution is 'incomplete.'
stories.opinion: A concrete, technically grounded move that highlights the fundamental tension between OS-level AI agents and end-to-end encrypted messaging. The acknowledged incompleteness makes it honest rather than performative.

stories.title: Everyday users are using AI coding tools to hack and customize their gadgets
stories.summary: A growing trend sees ordinary users employing AI coding tools like Claude Code and Codex to modify software on physical devices — TVs, cameras, and other gadgets. LLMs have dramatically lowered the barrier to hardware customization, as illustrated by a developer who used Claude Code to remove bloatware and redesign the interface on a Xiaomi Android TV over Wi-Fi.
stories.opinion: A vivid illustration of how AI coding tools are democratizing hardware tinkering, though the long-term implications for device security and warranty models are worth watching.

stories.title: South Korean education minister resigns after AI cheating scandal hits university exams
stories.summary: South Korea's education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned after an AI-assisted cheating scandal in university entrance exams. The crisis began when the top scorer on a national tax accountancy exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to cheat, sparking widespread fears about AI-enabled exam fraud.
stories.opinion: A striking early example of AI-enabled cheating causing real political consequences, likely a preview of challenges education systems worldwide will face.

stories.title: Nvidia faces contrasting narratives: strong earnings versus leadership uncertainty and China crackdown
stories.summary: Nvidia reported strong earnings with soaring revenue and impressive guidance under interim CEO Colette Kress, but prominent tech figures including Elon Musk are circulating a petition to bring back former CEO Jensen Huang, who says he's prepared to return. Nvidia's stock continues falling. Separately, Nvidia announced it will stop selling H200 chips to China and crack down on workarounds where Chinese companies remotely accessed chips in nearby countries like Malaysia, potentially affecting roughly 20% of Nvidia's business.
stories.opinion: A significant business story on multiple fronts — the leadership vacuum, the China enforcement, and the market's unease all compound into real strategic uncertainty for the most important AI hardware company.

stories.title: UN fails to agree on rules regulating autonomous weapons
stories.summary: UN diplomats in Geneva failed to produce legally binding rules on autonomous weapons, agreeing only to 'start discussing options.' Russia, Israel, and the US were the primary obstacles. A compromise gives countries two years to merely propose regulations, with actual negotiations expected to take much longer. The ICRC, UN Secretary-General, and Pope Leo had urged binding rules within one year.
stories.opinion: The added detail on US and Israeli obstruction alongside Russia, and the weak two-year compromise, makes the picture even bleaker than yesterday's report suggested. Where coverage differs: Guardian reports the talks 'collapsed' early Saturday after Russian objections could not be overcome; The Verge reports a compromise was reached giving countries two years to propose regulations, with Russia, Israel, and the US all cited as obstacles

stories.title: Column: GTA VI offers escape as real-world systems falter
stories.summary: Dave Schilling reflects on the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, drawing a parallel between real-world tech outages and systemic dysfunction and the appeal of escaping into a virtual world where players have some sense of control.
stories.opinion: A cultural commentary column loosely connected to tech; more about gaming culture than AI or technology news.

stories.title: AI agents that live in your text messages are a growing category
stories.summary: TechCrunch profiles several AI agents that work through text messaging rather than dedicated apps, including Ask Proxy, Caddy, Comma, Fambot, and the buzzy Instinct (valued at $10 billion after raising $1 billion). These agents handle scheduling, research, reservations, shopping, and task management through ordinary SMS, iMessage, RCS, Signal, and other messaging apps.
stories.opinion: The text-message-native AI agent space is heating up fast, with Instinct's $10B valuation signaling serious investor conviction that the messaging interface may win over dedicated apps.

tweet_headlines.author: crazyMLguy
tweet_headlines.headline: OpenUncensored abliterated Inkling 2 Mini's refusals by __modifying just 20 attention projection tensors__ — MMLU score barely moved, 78.95% → 79.47%.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
𝗜𝗻𝗸𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝟮 𝗠𝗶𝗻𝗶 𝗨𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗱: 𝗥𝗲𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗥𝗲𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗹𝘀 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴

OpenUncensored has released an abliterated version of Thinking Machine's Inkling 2 Mini.

What's interesting is the engineering behind it:

Uses directional ablation to remove refusal behavior.
Modifies just 20 attention projection tensors.
Preserves the original 26B MoE architecture with 3.4B active parameters.
MMLU score remains virtually unchanged: 78.95% → 79.47%.
Supports vision and 1M-token context.

In their evaluation, refusals dropped from 32/32 to 0/32 tested prompts.

An interesting demonstration of how targeted weight modifications can change model behavior without traditional fine-tuning.

Model: https://t.co/wJqXxWn51T

#LLM #OpenSource #AI #MachineLearning

tweet_headlines.author: orenoa7
tweet_headlines.headline: orenoa7's RTX 5090 benchmarks show Inkling 2 Mini fires __~6× more GPU kernel calls per token than Gemma__ — the likely reason its MoE advantage doesn't translate to speed yet.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Inkling 2 Mini 26B A5Bを早速実測！同じサイズ帯のGemma 4 26B-A4B、Qwen3.8 27BとRTX5090で比較

結果としてはMoEだから爆速！とはならず現状のllama.cpp実装だと速度がQwen3.8 27B Denseと同等の速度となった

■ Inklingの計測結果
256K入力時
・Prefill：1630 tok/s
・Prose：43 tok/s
・Code：57 tok/s

Gemma 4 26B-A4B比：
Prefill 49% / Prose 32% / Code 32%
Qwen3.8 27B比：
Prefill 120% / Prose 82% / Code 82%

今回llama.cppでそのまま動かしたが最適化しだいで改善の余地はありそう
RTX 3060 12GBとDGX SparkのInklingは計測中

■ なぜInklingは高速にならないのか
Inklingは中央12層を3回ループ実行する構造でアクティブ3.4Bに対しループ込みでは5.4B相当
それでもGemmaよりかなり遅い理由をnsysで調べた

Prefill
・Gemma4 26B A4Bにはない非量子化の行列演算が存在
・CPUからGPUへattentionの参照表の転送が発生していると推測

Decode
・1トークンあたりの kernel 呼び出しが Gemma の約6倍（約7370回に対してGemmaは約1,260回）

これらが速度差の一因になっている可能性がある

■ 256K Prefillの処理時間内訳
・Gemma：attentionが約8割
・Inkling：attentionは約2割で、残りはattention以外の処理
・実際に8K→256KでのPrefill低下は
Gemma -69%（10948→3350 tok/s）
Inkling -22%（2082→1630 tok/s）

■ 前提条件
モデル：
Unsloth GGUF
・Inkling 2 Mini (UD-Q4_K_XL 17.6GB)
・Gemma 4 26B-A4B (QAT UD-Q4_K_XL 14.2GB)
・Qwen3.8 27B (UD-Q4_K_XL 17.7GB)

ドラフト：
3モデルともON
・Inkling：公式dspark
・Gemma / Qwen：MTP

推論エンジン：
unsloth/llama.cpp b12588-mix-c0c3de8
(Inkling対応版をビルド / 3モデル共通)

ハードウェア：
RTX 5090 32GB (400W) / 全てGPU

計測：
1リクエスト / 出力1024 / greedy
思考OFF / ctx 262144
入力は文章とコード / 各点5回の中央値
KV：f16
・Qwenだけq8_0
・f16だと256KでVRAM 32GBに入らない

tweet_headlines.author: p0
tweet_headlines.headline: Independent benchmarks rank Inkling 2 Mini __#1 on cost efficiency__ at $25.80 per correct answer — and it gains more from adding web search than any other model tested.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
NEW: Inkling 2 Mini is the most efficient model we've tested:

- #1 on efficiency (cost vs. intelligence)
- #9 on intelligence (78.4) overall
- #1 on intelligence among open-weights models
- Lowest cost per correct answer ($25.80)
- Biggest accuracy gain from adding web search

It uses a looped transformer, which runs its middle layers three times for every token. That lets a 26B-parameter model reason more without generating more tokens, which keeps costs low. A model that size can't store as many facts, so it relies on search to fill the gaps, and that's where it gains the most.

tweet_headlines.headline: __Exactly How Much RAM You Need__ to Run Inkling-2-Mini on Your Laptop, by Quantization Level
tweet_headlines.source_text:
For folks wondering whether your laptop can run Inkling-2-Mini, there's a nice guide by @UnslothAI 

Note that you can run it on devices with as little as 9 GB of RAM, depending on the size you choose! Here are the memory requirements by size (expressed as bits):

1-bit: 9 GB
2-bit: 10-11 GB
3-bit: 13-15 GB
4-bit: 17-18 GB
8-bit: 24 GB

A larger size (more bits) means better performance but also uses more memory, which can slow it down.

Personally, I run the 3-bit version on my MacBook :)

tweet_headlines.author: PawelHuryn
tweet_headlines.headline: Pawel Huryn found that __55–85% of his Claude usage__ was the agent re-reading its own history — his fix: start each phase fresh with a shared STATUS.md file.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
In case long agent sessions are eating your Claude usage:
In mine, 55% to 85% of it was the agent re-reading its own history.

Now each phase of a long build starts in a fresh session, with my free /flight-deck skill: https://t.co/VSLGyLdeCP

Why it pays off: in one long session, every turn re-reads the whole conversation. 2x the length costs about 4x to re-read.

Why not just compact? Compaction lives inside one session of one tool, in the provider's format. My builds run across Claude Code, Codex and fresh review sessions. So the state lives in a file I own: STATUS.md, rewritten at the end of each phase with what's running, what's blocked and what's next. Any session in any tool can read it.

MIT. If it helps, star the repo.
